title: The insects' cousins
intro: Not every little critter is an insect. Let's meet their cousins —spiders, scorpions, centipedes, millipedes and pill bugs— and learn not to be afraid of them.

lessons.title: Arthropods: one big family
lessons.intro: Not every little critter is an insect. Today you'll meet the big arthropod family… and learn to count legs!
lessons.closing: Insects, spiders, scorpions, centipedes, millipedes and pill bugs are cousins: they all wear their skeleton on the outside. Counting legs tells you who's who!

exercises.prompt: Make pairs: match each animal with its legs.
exercises.explanation: Counting legs is the quickest clue to who's who: 6 means an insect, 8 a spider, 14 a pill bug, and lots and lots, a centipede or a millipede.

exercises.prompt: What do all arthropods have in common?
options: A skeleton on the outside and jointed legs
exercises.explanation: That's why they're one family: they wear armor on the outside and their legs bend in sections. Only many insects have wings, and spiders don't even have antennae.

exercises.prompt: Tap the ones that are arthropods.
exercises.explanation: The frog and the bird have their skeleton on the inside, like us, so they aren't arthropods. The other four wear their armor on the outside and have jointed legs.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: To grow, arthropods ___ their skeleton, because they have it ___.
exercises.explanation: Hard armor can't stretch: so they take off the old one and a new, bigger one grows underneath. That's shedding, or molting.

exercises.prompt: Count legs and put each one in its box.
exercises.explanation: With 6 legs it's an insect; with 8, an arachnid (a scorpion's pincers aren't legs); and with more than 8, another cousin: a centipede, a millipede or a pill bug.

lessons.title: Spiders
lessons.intro: Lots of people are scared of spiders, but it's almost always because we don't know them. Let's get to know them!
lessons.closing: A spider isn't an insect, but it's a great ally: it hunts mosquitoes and flies. Its web is a trap… and a work of art, too!

exercises.prompt: Put each name in its place on the spider.
exercises.explanation: A spider has only two parts: in front, the cephalothorax, which is head and thorax together and where its 8 legs come out; behind, the abdomen, where it makes silk.

exercises.prompt: Whose clue is it?
exercises.explanation: An insect has 6 legs, 3 parts (head, thorax and abdomen) and antennae. A spider has 8 legs, only 2 parts and no antennae: that's why it's an arachnid and not an insect.

exercises.prompt: Tap the part of the body where the spider makes silk.
exercises.explanation: Silk is made in the abdomen and comes out through the spinnerets, tiny tubes at its tip. That's why, when it spins, the spider lets the thread out from behind.

exercises.prompt: Why does a spider spin its web?
options: To catch insects and eat them
exercises.explanation: A web is a trap with sticky threads: when an insect gets caught, the spider feels the thread shake with its legs and goes to get it. It doesn't make it against us.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: Almost all spiders are ___ to people and they eat ___ and flies.
exercises.explanation: A spider in a corner of the garden is a hunter that works for free: every day it catches insects that bite or bother us, like mosquitoes, flies and cockroaches.

lessons.title: Spiders: looking without fear
lessons.intro: Are you scared of spiders? That's normal. Today you'll see why almost all of them are harmless and what to do about the few that aren't.
lessons.closing: Now you know: almost all spiders are shy and harmless. Looking without touching and telling an adult when needed: that's being brave!

exercises.prompt: True or false? Most spiders can't harm a person.
exercises.explanation: True: almost all of them are very small or have venom that's too weak for us. Their venom is for hunting insects, not for attacking people.

exercises.prompt: What do we do with each spider?
bins: Watch from a distance and tell an adult

sortItems.label: Black widow: shiny black with red marks
Recluse spider: brown, in a dark corner

exercises.explanation: You can calmly watch almost all of them without touching. The few dangerous ones, and any spider you don't know, are watched from a distance and you tell an adult: that way you're safe, and so is the spider.

exercises.prompt: There's a spider in your room. Put the steps in order to take it out without hurting it.

steps.label: The adult covers it with a glass and slides a piece of card underneath
They let it go outside, among the plants

exercises.explanation: With the glass and the card the spider is trapped without being squashed, and outside it can keep hunting insects. An adult does it, in case it's one that bites.

exercises.prompt: Make pairs: match each situation with the best thing to do.

pairs.left: You're about to put on shoes that were stored away
You see a black spider with red marks
pairs.right: Move away and tell an adult

pairs.left: You're looking for something in a dark corner
pairs.right: Look before you put your hand in

pairs.left: You see a web with dew in the garden
pairs.right: Look at it without breaking it

exercises.explanation: Spiders look for dark, quiet places to hide, like shoes and corners. If you look first and shake out your clothes, neither you nor the spider gets a fright.

exercises.prompt: If a spider bites you, what do you do?
options: I tell an adult right away
I look for the spider to squash it
exercises.explanation: Most of the time it's nothing, but an adult will know whether to wash the bite or go to the doctor. And remember: a spider only bites when it feels trapped, so it's best not to touch them.

lessons.title: Centipedes and millipedes
lessons.intro: They have so many legs it seems impossible to count them. But there's a trick to tell the centipede from the millipede.
lessons.closing: The centipede hunts and the millipede recycles: both help the garden. Watch the centipede from a distance; leave the millipede in peace with its leaves.

exercises.prompt: Centipede or millipede? Put each clue in its box.

sortItems.label: One pair of legs on each ring
Can bite: watch it from a distance
Two pairs of legs on each ring

exercises.explanation: The trick is in the rings: a centipede has one pair of legs on each and runs to hunt; a millipede has two pairs, moves slowly and curls up to protect itself.

exercises.prompt: Tap the centipede's head: that's where its antennae and hunting claws are.
exercises.explanation: The head is at the end where the two antennae come out. Next to its mouth it has venomous claws to catch insects: that's why you watch a centipede from a distance.

exercises.prompt: True or false? A centipede has exactly one hundred legs.
exercises.explanation: False: depending on the kind, it has from 30 to more than 300 legs, but never exactly one hundred. Its name just means “lots of legs”.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: A millipede has ___ pairs of legs on almost every ring and eats ___.
exercises.explanation: By eating dead leaves and rotting wood, the millipede turns them into new soil for plants: it's a soil recycler.

exercises.prompt: Make pairs.

pairs.right: Curls up like a snail shell
Each little piece of its long body

exercises.explanation: Centipedes and millipedes are myriapods: they have a long body made of many rings, and lots and lots of legs. One is a night hunter, and the other curls up when it's scared.

lessons.title: Pill bugs and scorpions
lessons.intro: One rolls into a ball and the other has pincers and a tail with a stinger. Neither of them is an insect: let's see whose cousins they are!
lessons.closing: The pill bug recycles and the scorpion hunts bugs at night. You can look at a pill bug up close; a scorpion, from a distance and telling an adult.

exercises.prompt: Which group does the pill bug belong to?
exercises.explanation: Even though it lives on land, the pill bug is a cousin of shrimp: it has 14 legs and breathes with special gills, which is why it needs damp places.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: The pill bug lives under stones and flowerpots because it needs ___, and when it's scared it rolls into a ___.
exercises.explanation: Its gills have to stay damp to breathe, so it looks for dark, wet places. Rolled into a ball, its armor protects it on every side.

exercises.prompt: Pill bug or scorpion? Put each clue in its box.

sortItems.label: Has a stinger on its tail

exercises.explanation: The pill bug is a recycling crustacean with 14 legs. The scorpion is an arachnid, like the spider: 8 legs, pincers to grab its prey and a stinger at the tip of its tail.

exercises.prompt: You see a scorpion in the yard. What do you do?
options: I move away and tell an adult
I grab it by the tail
I put it in a jar
exercises.explanation: Some scorpions in Venezuela have strong venom, especially for children. Moving away and telling an adult is the safest thing for you… and for the scorpion too.

exercises.prompt: Tap the ones that are arachnids.
exercises.explanation: Arachnids have 8 legs and no antennae: the spider and the scorpion. The pill bug is a crustacean, the fly an insect and the millipede a myriapod.

lessons.title: Insect or cousin?
lessons.intro: Today you're a detective: count legs, look at the body parts and listen carefully. Insect or cousin?
lessons.closing: Now you can tell insects from their cousins! Each one has its job, and none of them needs us to be afraid: just respectful.

exercises.prompt: Insect or cousin? Put each one in its box.
exercises.explanation: Insects have 6 legs and 3 parts. The spider and the scorpion have 8 legs, the millipede lots and lots, and the pill bug 14: they're cousins, but not insects.

exercises.prompt: Who's making that sound? An insect or not? Listen and choose.
options: A frog: it's not an insect
exercises.explanation: It's a frog: it croaks by puffing up an air sac in its throat. It's an amphibian, with its skeleton on the inside, so it's not an insect or an arthropod. A cricket, on the other hand, sings by rubbing its wings.

exercises.prompt: Make pairs: match each animal with its group.
exercises.explanation: They're four groups of the same arthropod family: insects with 6 legs, arachnids with 8, myriapods with lots and lots, and crustaceans like the pill bug, with 14.

exercises.prompt: You find a critter with 8 legs, no antennae and a body in 2 parts. What is it?
exercises.explanation: 8 legs, 2 parts and no antennae are the clues for arachnids. An insect would have 6 legs and antennae, and a myriapod, lots and lots of legs.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: They all have a job: the spider ___ mosquitoes, and the millipede and the pill bug ___ dead leaves.
exercises.explanation: None of them is extra: the hunters keep biting and pesky bugs in check, and the recyclers turn leaves into soil for plants.

exam.title: Unit challenge
exam.intro: The cousins challenge! Count legs, look at body parts and remember how to live alongside them without fear.
exam.closing: Well done, forest ranger! You know the insects' cousins and you know almost none of them is dangerous. With calm and respect, they all have their place.

exercises.prompt: Make pairs: match each animal with its legs.
exercises.explanation: Counting legs is the first clue: 6 for insects, 8 for arachnids, 14 for the pill bug and lots and lots for myriapods.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: All arthropods have their skeleton on the ___ and legs with ___.
exercises.explanation: Their outside armor protects them, and the joints let their legs bend in sections. We, on the other hand, have our skeleton on the inside.

exercises.prompt: Put each name in its place on the spider.
exercises.explanation: Two parts: the cephalothorax, where the 8 legs come out, and the abdomen, where silk is made.

exercises.prompt: Who's making that sound? An insect or not? Listen and choose.
options: A frog: it's not an insect
exercises.explanation: It's a cricket: the male sings by rubbing one wing against the other, like a violin. It's an insect: 6 legs, 3 parts and antennae.

exercises.prompt: Complete the sentence.
exercises.sentence: If there's a spider in the house, an adult covers it with a ___ and slides a ___ underneath to take it out.
exercises.explanation: That way the spider leaves the house without anyone getting hurt, and outside it keeps hunting mosquitoes and flies.

exercises.prompt: Centipede or millipede? Put each clue in its box.

sortItems.label: One pair of legs on each ring
Two pairs of legs on each ring
Eats dead leaves and curls up

exercises.explanation: The centipede, with one pair per ring, is a fast hunter; the millipede, with two pairs, is a slow recycler that curls up to protect itself.

exercises.prompt: Which group does the pill bug belong to?
exercises.explanation: It's a land crustacean: it has 14 legs and breathes with special gills that need moisture. That's why it lives under stones and flowerpots.

exercises.prompt: You see a scorpion in the yard. What do you do?
options: I move away and tell an adult
I grab it by the tail
I put it in a jar
exercises.explanation: Some scorpions in Venezuela have strong venom, especially for children: watch from a distance and tell an adult. And if one stings you, you need to go to the doctor.

exercises.prompt: Tap the ones that are insects.
exercises.explanation: The bee, the ladybug and the grasshopper have 6 legs and 3 parts: they're insects. The spider (8 legs), the pill bug (14) and the centipede (lots and lots) are their cousins.

exercises.prompt: What does a good forest ranger do with the insects' cousins?
options: Watches them with respect, doesn't touch the ones that can bite or sting, and tells an adult if needed
Is afraid of all of them
exercises.explanation: Almost all of them are harmless and help us by hunting bugs or recycling leaves. With the few dangerous ones, it's enough to know them, watch from a distance and tell an adult.
